Heat leaves a wall, stress moves through a beam, solute spreads through a
river, and pressure drives flow through a pipe. Different materials, different
scales, different equations on the page. Underneath, the same move repeats:
write what is conserved, write how the material responds, and let the field
describe the rest.

Structural analysis, heat transfer, porous flow, and contaminant transport do
not share the same units or applications. They share the same mathematical
architecture.

The architecture has two parts. A **conservation law** says something cannot
appear or disappear except through flow across a boundary or production inside
the region. A **constitutive law** says how the material responds: how heat
flows down a temperature gradient, how solute diffuses down a concentration
gradient, how stress relates to strain in a simple elastic solid.

---

## The local balance law

Take a small control volume inside a body, pipe, soil column, or fluid region.
Let $u$ be the amount of something stored per unit volume. Depending on the
problem, $u$ might be thermal energy, mass concentration, momentum density, or
another conserved quantity.

Let $\mathbf{q}$ be the **flux** of that quantity. Flux is a vector quantity:
its magnitude measures how much passes through a unit area per unit time, and
its direction is the direction of net transport.

The generic local balance law is

$$\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q} = s$$

where:

- $\partial u/\partial t$ is the local rate of storage
- $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{q}$ is the net outward flux
- $s$ is a source term

This one line is the template behind most continuum modelling. Change the
meaning of $u$, $\mathbf{q}$, and $s$, and you get a different physical
system. The bookkeeping structure stays the same.
This means the conservation architecture is reusable: once you understand the
balance law, many different physical theories become variations on one pattern.

The divergence term matters because a continuum model is local. It does not ask
"how much crossed the outer boundary of the whole pipe?" first. It asks what is
happening in an arbitrarily small piece. Once the local law is right, the
global law follows by integration.

    return { g, line, tip1, tip2 };

  const inArrow = makeArrow("#2563eb");

  const srcArrow = makeArrow("#7c3aed");

  const caption = document.createElement("p");
  caption.style.cssText = "font-size:0.9rem; color:#4b5563; margin:0.55rem 0 0 0;";

  function setArrow(obj, x1, y1, x2, y2, width) {
    obj.line.setAttribute("x1", x1);
    obj.line.setAttribute("y1", y1);
    obj.line.setAttribute("x2", x2);
    obj.line.setAttribute("y2", y2);

    const dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;

    const ux = dx / len, uy = dy / len;
    const bx = x2 - 12 * ux, by = y2 - 12 * uy;
    obj.tip1.setAttribute("x1", x2);
    obj.tip1.setAttribute("y1", y2);
    obj.tip1.setAttribute("x2", bx - 6 * uy);
    obj.tip1.setAttribute("y2", by + 6 * ux);
    obj.tip1.setAttribute("stroke-width", width);
    obj.tip2.setAttribute("x1", x2);
    obj.tip2.setAttribute("y1", y2);
    obj.tip2.setAttribute("x2", bx + 6 * uy);
    obj.tip2.setAttribute("y2", by - 6 * ux);
    obj.tip2.setAttribute("stroke-width", width);
  }

  function redraw() {
    inflow = parseFloat(inRow.input.value);

    outRow.out.textContent = outflow.toFixed(1);

    const m = MODES[mode];

    labels.store.textContent = m.store;
    labels.bar.textContent = "storage";
    labels.in.setAttribute("x", "115");

    labels.in.setAttribute("text-anchor", "middle");
    labels.in.textContent = m.fluxIn;
    labels.out.setAttribute("x", "445");
    labels.out.setAttribute("y", "120");
    labels.out.setAttribute("text-anchor", "middle");
    labels.out.textContent = m.fluxOut;
    labels.src.setAttribute("x", "280");
    labels.src.setAttribute("y", "48");
    labels.src.setAttribute("text-anchor", "middle");
    labels.src.textContent = m.source;

    setArrow(inArrow, 80, 130, 198, 130, arrowWidth(inflow));
    setArrow(outArrow, 362, 130, 440, 130, arrowWidth(outflow));
    if (source >= 0) {
      setArrow(srcArrow, 280, 30, 280, 68, arrowWidth(source));
    } else {
      setArrow(srcArrow, 280, 68, 280, 30, arrowWidth(source));
    }

    const fillH = 25 + 95 * clamp((acc + 10) / 20, 0, 1);
    barFill.setAttribute("x", "470");
    barFill.setAttribute("y", 190 - fillH);
    barFill.setAttribute("width", "42");
    barFill.setAttribute("height", fillH);
    barFill.setAttribute("fill", acc >= 0 ? "rgba(245,158,11,0.65)" : "rgba(239,68,68,0.65)");

    eqBox.textContent = `${inflow.toFixed(1)} - ${outflow.toFixed(1)} + ${source.toFixed(1)}`;
    rateBox.textContent = `${acc >= 0 ? "+" : ""}${acc.toFixed(1)} ${m.units}`;
    rateBox.style.color = acc >= 0 ? "#b45309" : "#b91c1c";
    stateBox.textContent = acc > 0 ? "storage rises" : acc < 0 ? "storage falls" : "balanced";
    caption.textContent = `In one-dimensional bookkeeping form, the local balance reads accumulation = inflow − outflow + source. The same geometry applies across heat, solute, and mass transport.`;
  }

  [inRow.input, outRow.input, srcRow.input].forEach(el => el.addEventListener("input", redraw));
  select.addEventListener("change", redraw);

  container.append(controls, modeRow, readout, svg, caption);
  redraw();
  return container;
}

## Constitutive laws

A balance law tells you what must be accounted for. It does not say how the
material responds. That extra relation is the constitutive law.

Two standard examples are:

**Fourier's law of heat conduction**

$$\mathbf{q} = -k\nabla T$$

Heat flux points down the temperature gradient. The constant $k$ is thermal
conductivity. The minus sign means heat flows from hot to cold.

**Fick's law of diffusion**

$$\mathbf{J} = -D\nabla c$$

Mass flux points down the concentration gradient. The constant $D$ is the
diffusivity.

The structure is the same in both. A gradient creates a driving force. The
material constant tells you how strongly the medium responds.

In elementary elasticity, the constitutive law is often written as a linear
stress-strain relation. In one dimension,

$$\sigma = E\varepsilon$$

where $\sigma$ is **stress** (force per unit area, Pa), $\varepsilon$ is
**strain** (fractional change in length, dimensionless), and $E$ is Young's
modulus (the material stiffness).

The structure is the same: one field quantity is related to another by a
material response parameter.

This 1D relation extends to three dimensions as a tensor equation relating the
full strain tensor to the full stress tensor through a stiffness matrix. The
scalar form here captures the logic; discipline courses in mechanics of
materials and structural analysis build out the three-dimensional version.

## Why signs and directions matter

Continuum laws are full of minus signs, outward normals, and directional
derivatives. These are not decorative details. They are the physics.

If temperature increases to the right, then $\nabla T$ points right. Fourier's
law says the heat flux points left. Miss the minus sign and you literally model
heat flowing from cold to hot.

The same applies to every constitutive law in this chapter. Continuum
mathematics is geometry with units attached. Direction is part of the answer.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Where the PDE comes from

Conservation laws come from bookkeeping on a region. Constitutive laws come
from empirical or theoretical descriptions of how a material responds. The PDE
appears when you combine them.

For example, if thermal energy density is proportional to temperature and heat
flux obeys Fourier's law, then storage plus divergence of heat flux produces the
heat equation. The PDE is not the starting point. It is the compressed result
of conservation plus material behaviour.
:::

## The core method

A first pass through a continuum or transport problem usually goes like this:

1. Identify the conserved quantity: mass, energy, momentum, or solute.
2. Write the local balance law for storage, flux, and source.
3. Choose the constitutive law that links flux or stress to the driving field.
4. Substitute the constitutive law into the balance law.
5. Inspect the resulting PDE or field equation and connect each term back to a
   physical mechanism.
6. Add boundary and initial conditions only after the governing structure is
   clear.

That last point matters. Students often see the PDE first and the modelling
logic second. In upper-year work, reversing that order helps. If you know where
every term came from, the equation stops feeling arbitrary.

## Worked example 1: heat conduction in one dimension

Let $T(x,t)$ be temperature in a rod. Suppose there is no internal heat source.
The local energy balance says:

$$\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q} = 0$$

In one dimension, thermal energy per unit volume is $u = \rho c_p T$, where
$\rho$ is mass density (kg m$^{-3}$) and $c_p$ is specific heat capacity
(J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$). Substituting into the generic balance law gives

$$\rho c_p \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial q}{\partial x} = 0$$

Use Fourier's law in one dimension:

$$q = -k\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}$$

Substitute:

$$\rho c_p \frac{\partial T}{\partial t}
 - \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(k\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}\right) = 0$$

If $k$ is constant, this simplifies to

$$\rho c_p \frac{\partial T}{\partial t}
 = k\frac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2}$$

or

$$\frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \alpha \frac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2},
\qquad \alpha = \frac{k}{\rho c_p}$$

This is the heat equation. The second spatial derivative tells you how much the
temperature field differs from its local linear trend. Where the field is
strongly curved, temperature changes quickly in time.

## Worked example 2: contaminant diffusion in groundwater

Let $c(x,t)$ be solute concentration in a one-dimensional porous medium. Ignore
advection for the moment and assume no chemical reaction source.

The balance law is

$$\frac{\partial c}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial J}{\partial x} = 0$$

Use Fick's law:

$$J = -D\frac{\partial c}{\partial x}$$

Substitute:

$$\frac{\partial c}{\partial t}
 - \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(D\frac{\partial c}{\partial x}\right)=0$$

For constant diffusivity:

$$\frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = D\frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial x^2}$$

This has the same structure as the heat equation. Physically the fields mean
something different — but the mathematical skeleton is shared. Recognising
that is most of what this chapter is for.

In real groundwater and river-transport problems, advection — the bulk
movement of solute carried by flowing water — usually dominates or competes
with diffusion. In the generic framework, advection enters through the flux
term: the total flux is $J = vc - D\,\partial c/\partial x$, where $vc$ is
the solute carried by the bulk flow and $-D\,\partial c/\partial x$ is the
diffusive part from Fick's law. Substituting into the balance law and
rearranging gives

$$\frac{\partial c}{\partial t} + v\frac{\partial c}{\partial x}
 = D\frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial x^2}$$

The pure-diffusion case here applies when the pore velocity is low (dense clay,
for example) or when setting up an initial model to isolate the diffusive
contribution before adding flow. The full advection-diffusion equation is taken
up in environmental and geotechnical engineering courses.

## Worked example 3: linear elasticity in one dimension

Take a slender bar under axial load. In the simplest small-strain setting,
strain is

$$\varepsilon = \frac{dw}{dx}$$

where $w(x)$ is axial displacement (using $w$ to avoid confusion with the
generic stored quantity $u$ used earlier). Hooke's law gives

$$\sigma = E\varepsilon = E\frac{dw}{dx}$$

In the generic framework, stress plays the role of flux: it is the quantity that
transmits the internal load across a cross-section. The "storage" term vanishes
in static equilibrium, so the balance law reduces to a divergence-only statement
with a source. The general 1D force balance in a body with distributed body
force $b$ (force per unit volume, e.g. self-weight, corresponding to the source
term $s$ in the generic law) is

$$\frac{d\sigma}{dx} + b = 0$$

If body forces are negligible ($b = 0$), this reduces to

$$\frac{d\sigma}{dx} = 0$$

Substitute the constitutive relation:

$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(E\frac{dw}{dx}\right) = 0$$

For constant $E$:

$$E\frac{d^2w}{dx^2} = 0 \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \frac{d^2w}{dx^2} = 0$$

This is much simpler than the heat and diffusion examples, but the logic is the
same. Balance law plus constitutive law gives the governing equation.

## Where this goes

The most direct continuation is
[Computational methods for engineering models](04-computational-methods.qmd).
Once the governing equations are written, most upper-year work shifts from
derivation to solution. Real geometries, mixed materials, and realistic
boundary conditions usually push these problems toward numerical methods,
meshes, and solver design.

Environmental transport, remote sensing inversion, and geophysics all use the
same structure. The quantity and units change. The control-volume logic does
not.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Applications

- heat flow through walls, fins, and machine components
- diffusion and mixing in process equipment
- contaminant transport in groundwater and rivers
- stress and deformation in structural members
- porous flow and subsurface energy transport
- continuum models in earth and environmental systems
:::

## Exercises

Each exercise asks you to derive a governing equation. State the physical
meaning of each term as well as the final equation.

### Exercise 1

Starting from the one-dimensional heat balance

$$\rho c_p \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial q}{\partial x} = 0$$

and Fourier's law

$$q = -k\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}$$

derive the heat equation for constant $k$.

steps:
  - op: "Write the constitutive law in displacement form"
    eq: "\\sigma = E\\frac{dw}{dx}"
    note: "Stress is proportional to strain, and strain is the displacement gradient."
  - op: "Substitute into equilibrium"
    eq: "\\frac{d}{dx}\\left(E\\frac{dw}{dx}\\right) = 0"
    note: "Balance is written in terms of stress, so substitute stress first."
  - op: "Use constant modulus"
    eq: "E\\frac{d^2w}{dx^2} = 0"
    note: ~
  - op: "Simplify"
    eq: "\\frac{d^2w}{dx^2} = 0"
    note: "Because E is nonzero and constant."
  - op: "Check"
    eq: "\\text{balance plus constitutive law gives the displacement equation}"
    note: "This is the same modelling pattern as the transport examples."
-->

### Exercise 4

Choose one field setting from your own area: a wall, pipe, aquifer, beam, soil
column, battery, or river reach.

Prepare a one-page systems sketch naming:

1. the conserved quantity
2. the flux
3. the constitutive law
4. one plausible source term
5. one important boundary condition
6. one reason the resulting equation will probably need numerical solution

<!-- VIZ: Constitutive-law comparison board. Show three side-by-side panels for heat conduction, diffusion, and 1D elasticity. Each panel should display the field, gradient, flux or stress, and governing equation, with matching visual structure and labels so the reader can see the parallel mathematics rather than three separate subjects. -->

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  function svgEl(tag) { return document.createElementNS("http://www.w3.org/2000/svg", tag); }
  const container = document.createElement("div");
  container.style.cssText = "max-width: 900px; margin: 1rem 0 1.25rem 0; font-family: inherit;";
  const board = document.createElement("div");
  board.style.cssText = "display:grid; grid-template-columns:repeat(3,minmax(0,1fr)); gap:0.75rem;";
  const models = [
    { title: "Heat conduction", field: "temperature T", grad: "∇T", response: "q = -k∇T", eq: "∂T/∂t = αTxx", color: "#2563eb", left: "hot", right: "cold" },
    { title: "Diffusion", field: "concentration c", grad: "∇c", response: "J = -D∇c", eq: "∂c/∂t = Dcxx", color: "#059669", left: "high c", right: "low c" },
    { title: "Elasticity", field: "displacement u", grad: "ε = ux", response: "σ = Eε", eq: "σx + f = 0", color: "#f59e0b", left: "stretch", right: "relax" }
  ];
  models.forEach(model => {
    const panel = document.createElement("div");
    panel.style.cssText = "background:#fff; border:1px solid #e5e7eb; border-radius:10px; padding:0.7rem;";
    const h = document.createElement("div");
    h.style.cssText = "font-size:0.9rem; font-weight:700; color:#111827; margin-bottom:0.35rem;";
    h.textContent = model.title;
    const svg = svgEl("svg");
    svg.setAttribute("viewBox", "0 0 240 180");
    svg.setAttribute("width", "100%");
    svg.style.display = "block";
    const rect = svgEl("rect");
    rect.setAttribute("x", "28"); rect.setAttribute("y", "46"); rect.setAttribute("width", "160"); rect.setAttribute("height", "44");
    rect.setAttribute("fill", "#f8fafc"); rect.setAttribute("stroke", "#cbd5e1");
    svg.appendChild(rect);
    const grad = svgEl("line");
    grad.setAttribute("x1", "46"); grad.setAttribute("y1", "68"); grad.setAttribute("x2", "170"); grad.setAttribute("y2", "68");
    grad.setAttribute("stroke", model.color); grad.setAttribute("stroke-width", "3");
    svg.appendChild(grad);
    const arrow = svgEl("line");
    arrow.setAttribute("x1", "172"); arrow.setAttribute("y1", "68"); arrow.setAttribute("x2", "206"); arrow.setAttribute("y2", "68");
    arrow.setAttribute("stroke", model.color); arrow.setAttribute("stroke-width", "3");
    svg.appendChild(arrow);
    const tip1 = svgEl("line");
    tip1.setAttribute("x1", "206"); tip1.setAttribute("y1", "68"); tip1.setAttribute("x2", "196"); tip1.setAttribute("y2", "62");
    tip1.setAttribute("stroke", model.color); tip1.setAttribute("stroke-width", "3");
    svg.appendChild(tip1);
    const tip2 = svgEl("line");
    tip2.setAttribute("x1", "206"); tip2.setAttribute("y1", "68"); tip2.setAttribute("x2", "196"); tip2.setAttribute("y2", "74");
    tip2.setAttribute("stroke", model.color); tip2.setAttribute("stroke-width", "3");
    svg.appendChild(tip2);
    [["42","40",model.left],["174","40",model.right],["108","118",model.field],["205","61",model.response]].forEach(([x,y,t], idx) => {
      const text = svgEl("text");
      text.setAttribute("x", x); text.setAttribute("y", y);
      text.setAttribute("font-size", idx === 2 ? "12" : "11");
      text.setAttribute("fill", idx === 3 ? model.color : "#374151");
      text.setAttribute("text-anchor", idx === 2 ? "middle" : "start");
      text.textContent = t;
      svg.appendChild(text);
    });
    const eq = document.createElement("div");
    eq.style.cssText = "font-size:0.96rem; color:#111827; margin-top:0.45rem; font-family:serif;";
    eq.textContent = model.eq;
    const note = document.createElement("div");
    note.style.cssText = "font-size:0.85rem; color:#4b5563; margin-top:0.25rem;";
    note.textContent = `${model.grad} creates the response term. The governing law keeps the same structure while only the field names change.`;
    panel.append(h, svg, eq, note);
    board.appendChild(panel);
  });
  const caption = document.createElement("p");
  caption.style.cssText = "font-size:0.9rem; color:#4b5563; margin:0.55rem 0 0 0;";
  caption.textContent = "These are not three unrelated subjects. In each case, a field varies in space, a gradient is formed, and the material law converts that gradient into a flux or stress response.";
  container.append(board, caption);
  return container;
}
```
